recentItems.title: Polish tango 1935: Chór Juranda  - Jak trudno jest zapomnieć (How Hard It's To Forget)
recentItems.description:
Chór JURANDA (The Jurand’s Choir) – Jak trudno jest zapomnieć (How Hard It’s To Forget) Tango (Wars – Jurandot) z f-mu „Manewry miłosne” (From the film comedy The Love Manuevers) Syrena-Electro 1935 (Polish)

NOTE: This beautiful, melancholic composition is one of the finest tangos written in Poland during the second half of the 1930s. Its creator—the distinguished composer, pianist, and orchestra leader Henryk Wars—wrote it for the hit movie comedy “Manewry miłosne” (The Love Maneuvers). In the film, the piece is performed by Adam Aston (who plays the role of a wandering Gypsy musician), sung at a slow tempo in the style of a Russian romance. The film also features a constellation of stars from pre-war Polish comedy cinema, including Tola Mankiewiczówna, Mira Zimińska, Aleksander Żabczyński or Loda Halama. A colorized version of this film can be viewed on YouTube. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q0tvAGmtT-4&list=PLqewUcRHTDL9dvjihyyHoyh-0h6kEQ93P&index=14 

Chór JURANDA: The Jurand Choir was a popular Polish male vocal ensemble, founded in the early 1930s as a rival to the Dan Choir (Chór Dana)—the most prominent Polish revelers of that era. Before long, the Jurand Choir achieved a level of popularity on par with the Dan Choir and continued to perform successfully even in post-war Poland, albeit under a new name: the Czejand Choir (Chór Czejanda). The ensemble’s activity finally came to an end in 1956, with the arrival of the rock music era, which gradually eclipsed the popularity of such vocal groups from the past. 

The slideshow presents some photos of the life in pre-war Poland.

recentItems.title: Roaring Twenties: Hollywood Dance Orch. - In The Middle Of The Night, 1926
recentItems.description:
Hollywood Dance Orchesatra – In the Middle Of the Night, Waltz (Rose-Donaldson, with Vocal chorus by Hugh Donovan (alias Charles Harrison) Banner 1926 (USA)

NOTE:  Hollywood Dance Orchestra was a popular pseudonym for a multitude of American dance orchestras in the Roaring Twenties, recording for various off-mainstream labels (Banner, Crown, Domino, Imperial, Pathé Actuelle, Oriole, Regal). Many top-notch bandleaders used this pseudonym, including Nathan Glantz, B.A. Rolfe, Adrian Shubert, Joseph Samuels or  Sam Lanin, and I don't dare investigate who appears on this album. The vocalist Hugh Donovan is also a pseudonym of the American singer, Charles Harrison, who in the accoustic recording era  was the noted  Columbia artist performing in the operatic tenor repertoire, yet later he shifted to popular ballads and hits of the day to become entirely forgotten in the 1930s. 
Fortunately, Walter Donaldson uses his own name as the composer of this charming, slow waltz. Check the equally beautiful instrumental version of this tune  played by Vincent Lopez and his Casa Lopez Orchestr.  https://youtu.be/Ku2-H1Xb8_E

recentItems.title: Roaring Twenties: Roy Ingraham & His Orch. - Chant of the Jungle, 1929
recentItems.description:
Roy Ingraham & His Orchestra – Chant of the Jungle, Fox-Trot (Freed-Brown) from MGM film „Untamed”, with Vocal Trio, Brunswick 1929, USA

NOTE: Roy INGRAHAM (b. 1893, Whiting Indiana – d. 1988, LA California) – American composer, singer and dance band conductor. He was a vaudeville performer between 1916 and 1923, then he led a dance orchestra in California, and later at New York's Paramount Hotel Grill. He wrote songs for the Florentine Gardens for seven years, and also began working for films at this time. Ingraham’s s popular-song compositions include "No Regrets", "Deep In the Arms of Love", "On the Sunny Side of the Rockies", "I Sing All My Love Songs to You", "A Girl Like You, A Boy Like Me", and "Love Is a Beautiful Song".

recentItems.title: Roaring Twenties: Harry Archer & His Orch. - Lantern of Love, 1926
recentItems.description:
Harry ARCHER & His Orchestra - Lantern of Love, Fox-Trot from the Comedy „Castles In the Air” (Raymond W. Peck – Percy Wenrich) with Vocal chorus, Brunswick 1926 (USA)

NOTE: Harry ARCHER (born 1888 in Creston, Iowa - died 1960 in New York) American pianist, composer and dance  band leader. His band is best remembered for its hot jazzy dance recordings for Brunswick records through the mid-late 1920s. He is also known as the author of the hit songs and orchestration with Paul Whiteman's orchestra for the famous 1923/24 Broadway play "Little Jesse James."

recentItems.title: 1934: Janusz Popławski  - Sings Etude Żal (Regret) by Frederic Chopin
recentItems.description:
Janusz Popławski z Warszawską Ork. Symfoniczną  pod dyr. Ludomira Różyckiego (Tenor acc. by Warsaw Symphony Orch. dir. by Ludomir Różycki) – Żal („Regret”) Improvisation on Etude  E-flat Major,  op. 10 nr 3 (Fryderyk Chopin - Lyrics by M. Józefowicz), Columbia 1934 (Polish)

NOTE: This Chopin’s piece, with its contemplative mood, resonates well with All Saints' Day—a holiday observed in Poland today with great solemnity. People gather in cemeteries at the graves of their loved ones—amidst falling, yellowed leaves—bringing bouquets of chrysanthemums and memorial candles, offering prayers, and recalling tender memories. This stands in stark contrast to the Halloween tradition rooted in Anglo-Saxon culture, with its fancy guises of devils and witches. Fortunately, such displays still remain absent in Polish cemeteries.

Janusz POPŁAWSKI (born 1898 in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski – died 1971 in Gliwice, Poland) was one of the most popular pre-war Polish radio singers. He also gained great acclaim through numerous recordings for Columbia, Odeon, and Cristall-Electro—ranging from current revue and film hits to major operetta and operatic tenor arias. Known as the "sunny tenor" due to the bright, joyful timbre of his voice, he could have become a leading opera star; also owing to his good physical presence and engaging appearance. However, he was active primarily in the light entertainment repertoire. In Sept. 1939 the outbreak of the  2nd World War  interrupted his  career. Popławski did not join the boycott—widespread among Polish artists—of theaters managed by the German occupiers. He continued to perform in 2nd rate German revues, a fact for which, for a number of years, he was banned to perform in Warsaw (a penalty for actors for breaking the boycott against the Germans during the Occupation). Popławski performed on provincial stages, including in Silesia (Gliwice), however he continued to record for the Muza label, often using the pseudonym Marian Olszewski  https://youtu.be/M4p97Jj-D3E  

I also recommend on my channel another  vocal version of Etude e-dur (E-flat Major)  recorded by Polish revelers 4 Asy (The Four Aces Choir - post-2WW successors of the Dana Choir).  https://youtu.be/Rqb4gktPLIc

recentItems.title: Ambrose & His Mayfair Hotel Orch. -- My Bluebird Was Caught In the Rain, 1930
recentItems.description:
Ambrose & His Orchestra at the May Fair Hotel, London – My Bluebird Was Caught In the Rain, Fox-Trot (Creamer & Rich) HMV 1930 (British)

NOTE: Benjamin Baruch („Bert”) AMBROSE (born 1896, Warsaw, Poland – died 1971, Leeds, UK) was a British dance orchestra leader, one of the most acclaimed London orchestra leaders of his time. Born in Warsaw to the family of a Jewish wool merchant, he settled with his family in East Ham, London, in the first decade of the 20th century. He learned to play the violin early in life and was taken to the US by his aunt at the age of 15. There he was hired as a violinist in Emil Coleman's famous dance orchestra in New York, and later played at the Palais Royal dance venue, until, at the age of 20, Bert was persuaded to form his own 15-piece band. However, in 1922, his mother became ill and he returned to Britain, where he formed a seven-piece band to play at the hugely popular West End restaurant, the Embassy Club. He demanded a weekly salary of £360, a huge sum of money at the time. The club was soon purchased by another restaurateur, who became Ambrose's business partner. During this period, Ambrose recorded his first 12 sides for Columbia Records. Despite a brief stint back in the US to play at New York's Clover Gardens, Bert Ambrose remained at the Embassy Club until 1927, when he was offered the opportunity to take over the dance orchestra at the newly opened May Fair Hotel in London. The contract included broadcasting, which brought Ambrose national fame. His band was Anglo-American and comprised top-notch musicians who could play in a wide variety of styles and improvise at will, such as John and Bert Firman and Jay Wilbur, to name just three. In June 1933, Ambrose returned to the Embassy Club for almost three years before embarking on a national tour in Jan 1936. Afterwards, he bought Ciro's Club in partnership with another American violinist and bandleader, Jack Harris. However, the two ambitious bandleaders, playing in rotation, could not stand each other for long, and the partnership fell apart. Ambrose moved to the Cafe de Paris until the outbreak of 2nd World War, which reduced the number of his musicians conscripted for military service. Ambrose returned to May Fair for a short contract, after which he retired in 1940, tired of the bombings and air raids and spending most of his time on his farm in Hertfordshire. He continued recording with his orchestra for Decca until 1947. In 1971, Bert Ambrose died suddenly of a stroke while preparing for a show at Yorkshire TV Studios.

SAM BROWNE, born in London, one of the most popular British dance band vocalists of the 1930's. He is particularly remembered singing with Ambrose and his Orchestra, at the Mayfair Hotel and Embassy Club, with whom he made many recordings from 1930 to 1942.

Appropriately to the “rainy” title, the slideshow features several photos of rainy days from yesteryear in various places of the world.

recentItems.title: Polish Tango 1937: Mieczysław Fogg & Iwo Wesby Orch. -  Spójrz [Look!]
recentItems.description:
Mieczysław Fogg & Ork. Iwo Wesby’ego – Spójrz (Look/ My Star Is Falling) or: (Look up/ at the swarm of stars ) Tango (Petersburski- Sewer) Syrena-Electro 1937 (Polish)

NOTE: This song, composed by the world-renowned Polish composer Jerzy Petersburski —who also wrote in 1929 the classic tango "Oh, Donna Clara" (in Polish "Tango Milonga")—never became a hit, even though it was recorded by the immensely popular Mieczysław Fogg and other well-known performers, such as Adam Aston. https://youtu.be/ILrD8UUdoes  The romantic chorus describes falling stars in the Venetian sky, when a pair of lovers travel along the canal, accompanied by the gentle splashing of oars. For this reason, the slideshow features views of beautiful Italian nights—starry, or not—captured in the vintage posters and photographs.

recentItems.title: Eugene Jaudas' Dance Band - Poor Butterfly, Fox-Trot 1916
recentItems.description:
Eugene Jaudas’ Band - Poor Butterfly (Raymond Hubbell) Fox-Trot, Edison (USA) 1916

NOTE: Eugene A. JAUDAS was an American violinist and dance band leader; between 1911 and 1920, he and his ensemble—Jaudas’ Band (also known as Jaudas’ Society Orchestra)—recorded for the Edison label, producing both early commercial phonograph cylinders and Diamond Discs. 

The famous song "Poor Butterfly" was composed in 1916 by Raymond Hubbell, who drew inspiration from Puccini’s opera *Madame Butterfly* (the composition includes a brief musical quote from the "Tutti i fior" duet, Act II). Featuring lyrics by John T. Golden, the song debuted on Broadway in the production “The Big Show”—staged at New York’s Hippodrome Theatre starting in August 1916—where it was performed by Sophie Bernard. By December of that same year, Edison had recorded—in addition to the instrumental dance version by Jaudas’ Band—two vocal interpretations: one by Elsie Baker (performing under the pseudonym Edna Brown) and another by Elizabeth Spencer. The piece went on to become a jazz standard, recorded in later years by numerous artists, including Paul Whiteman, Benny Goodman, Art Tatum, Erroll Garner, Deanna Durbin, Sarah Vaughan, Paul Desmond, Julie Andrews, and many others.

recentItems.title: Roaring Twenties: Arthur Briggs' Savoy Syncops Orch. - Vo-Do-Do-De-O Blues, 1927
recentItems.description:
Arthur Briggs’ Savoy Syncops’ Orchestra - Vo-Do-Do-De-O Blues (Yellen-Ager), Polydor 1927 (Rec. in Berlin, Austrian product)

NOTE: Arthur BRIGGS (b.1899, Charleston, S. Carolina, USA – d. 1991, Paris, France). Afro-American trumpeter and bandleader who performed in Europe primarily in the 1920s and 30s, when he formed in 1922 the Savoy Syncopators Orchestra in Belgium, and then became popular during the Roaring Twenties in Berlin and Paris. In 1928 the band broke up and Briggs recorded again in 1929 in Paris under the name of the Orchestre Arthur Briggs &  His Boys. In 1930 he joined the Noble Sissle Orchestra, when it performed in London and in USA. In 1931 Briggs was back in Paris, where he stayed until his death. In the 1930s he led various bands with the front-row musicians such as Coleman Hawkins, Django Reinhardt and Stéphane Grappelli. During the World War 2, Briggs was arrested in Paris and imprisoned in a German concentration camp, but he survived and after the liberation continued to play in Europe until the mid-1960s. Interesting detail is the cooperation of Arthur Briggs with the legendary British vocalist Al Bowlly, who as a beginner guitarist & vocalist happened to stay in the late 1920s. for some time in Berlin, which was then considered as European capital of jazz. Al Bowlly performed there during the tea dances as a crooner and occasionally recorded with Arthur Briggs a couple of sides for the Grammophon - and it’s when Al Bowlly’s voice for the first time was put on record.
The slideshow presents some awesome German & Austrian posters from the Roaring Twenties.

recentItems.title: Viva Maria! Pasodoble  - Ork. Godarskiego (aka Heinz Huppertz) 1940s
recentItems.description:
Godarski Orchestra (Heinz Huppertz Tanz-Orchester ?) - Viva Maria, Pasodoble (J.Rixner),  (Originally recorded in Germany in early 1940s, Polish release by Melodje (c. 1946)  

NOTE: In Soviet-occupied postwar Poland, "Godarski's Orchestra" was the label name of a fictitious dance band – a cover for pirated reissues of various pre-war and wartime international albums, as well as contemporary foreign dance groups with whom Poland had not signed a copyright. The first private Polish post-war record production Melodie, based in Poznań, was very prolific in releasing such pirated dance records, which were eagerly purchased until Melodje was closed down in 1948 by the Soviet bureaucrats and the state-owned Muza Records was established instead. Godarski's Orchestra most often covers German swing bands from the 1930s and 1940s, such as Michael Jary, Heinz Huppertz and others. To my ear, it's the latter who plays the paso doble "Viva Maria."

recentItems.title: 1930 Polish Apache Tango: [Ah, Don't Leave Me] Nie odchodź ode mnie - sung by Kazimierz Szerszyński
recentItems.description:
Kazimierz Szerszyński & Odeon Orchestra, cond. by Henryk Wars - "Nie odchodź ode mnie” (Don’t Go Away From Me!) Tango z rewii “Uśmiech Warszawy” teatru Morskie Oko (A.Gold – A. Włast) [Tango from the Morskie Oko revue "Uśmiech Warszawy" (The Smile of Warsaw)]  Odeon 1930 (Polish) 

NOTE: The Apache tango "Don't go away from me" was sung in the Morskie Oko theatre by Stanisława Nowicka, the queen of Polish tango. The lyrics wriitten by Andrzej Włast go like: “My lover is a bandit, drunkard, gambler / And not my tears nor my wails move him / Yet when he kisses me – he’s beautiful like god / his torso is powerful like the archer’s / so if he leaves me, my world will make no sense. Ah, don’t leave me / you heartless, you rascal / for if you do, I know / you will even more miss me!

It is  one of the most famous prewar hits  by Artur GOLD, brother of Henryk Gold - Warsaw's most popular dance bandleader of the 1930s. Artur wrote many famous Polish hits as "Ta mała jest wstawiona" (That little one is tipsy)  https://youtu.be/_gFT58tS0Is  , "Brawo Bis!" (Bravo Bis!)  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6j9DcF2Rj8Y  , "Ach te Cyganki!" (Ach these Gypsy girls!) https://youtu.be/jqSnkNnCOxM   , "Ja nie mam co na siebie włożyć" (I have simply nothing to wear!) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQfVL1ojj8o  , and the evergreen tangos "Szkoda twoich łez, dziewczyno" (There’s No Use Crying, My Girl) https://youtu.be/CppbkqUbk7A  "Oczy czarne" (Black eyes) https://youtu.be/oDmNJOS02w4    "Jesienne róże” (Autumn roses)  https://youtu.be/96enXCDXqHc  or "O przyjdź kochanku mój, blade usta daj” (O Come My Lover, Give Me Your Pale Lips) https://youtu.be/s6jlku0bryI   . Sent to the Nazi ghetto in Warsaw during the German occupation of Poland, Arthur Gold was murdered in the German extermination camp of Treblinka around 1943.


Kazimierz SZERSZYŃSKI (b. 1888 in Radom, Poland – died 1943 in Warsaw) was a Polish singer and actor. Born into a wine merchant's family, he studied tenor singing in the Warsaw Conservatory, but after graduating, he chose a lighter genre and got engaged in Warsaw comedy theatres: Modern (1912/13) and Bagatela (1914). He then toured Russia for 3 years, partnering the famous Polish vedette Wiktoria Kawecka, and after the outbreak of the Bolshevik Revolution in 1917, he moved to Paris. He performed in various Parisian cabarets until 1921, when he returned to Warsaw to appear in popular revue theatres Qui Pro Quo (1922/23) and Nowości (1924 and 1927/28). In the 1930s, he was hired by the Warsaw Operetta, and shortly before World War II, he began appearing in supporting roles in the movies, however he never gained any higher rank there. He died in Warsaw in 1943 during the German occupation. See one more Szerszyński’s performance in another famous Polish pre-war tango “Już Nigdy” (Never Again) https://youtu.be/zFiDWxr487k

recentItems.title: Hot Charleston!! 1926: Julian Fuhs Tanz-Orch. - Yours With Love And Kisses
recentItems.description:
Julian Fuhs und sein Orchester – Yours With Love And Kisses, Charleston (Davis-Silver), Electrola 1926 (German)

NOTE: Julian FUHS (b. 1891 in Berlin – d. 1975 in Miami, USA) German-American jazz pianist and dance band leader. After completing his musical education at the Stern Conservatory in Berlin, Julian Fuhs emigrated to the United States, where he became a U.S. citizen in 1916. He returned to Berlin in 1924 and founded the Follies Band, performing jazz and dance music in American style. His orchestra enjoyed immense success among the German elites of the Jazz Age—who were fascinated by American culture—and Fuhs himself played a significant role in popularizing jazz in Germany during the 1920s. At the peak of his career, he was considered the German counterpart to Paul Whiteman—particularly after recording his own version of Gershwin’s “Rhapsody in Blue”; he was the first artist to record the piece in Europe. Unfortunately, the Great Depression hit him hard, leading Fuhs to disband his orchestra in 1931. Moreover, shifts in American musical tastes paved the way for swing, while the hot-dance music of the Roaring Twenties began to fall out of fashion. Julian Fuhs withdrew from the music scene and opened a bar; however, two years later, the NSDAP rise to power in Germany forced him to leave the country in 1933. Fuhs traveled first to Austria and then to Prague and Paris, yet he was unable to successfully resume his musical career in any of these places. In 1937, he emigrated to the United States, where he also failed to replicate the success he had enjoyed in Europe during the 1920s. Forgotten and unable to find a place in the American big-band mainstream of the 1930s and 1940s, Julian Fuhs earned a living as a salesman and died in poverty.
